svg.title: Figure 3 | Execution Environment, Security and Observability
svg.desc: Check the working location, access boundaries and evidence: where execution happens, which data can be accessed and how results can be verified.

g.font-family: Arial, Noto Sans CJK TC, sans-serif
g.text: Figure 3 | Execution Environment, Security and Observability
4. Execution Environment: which computer is the engineer
working on?
Suppose the engineer uses the correct command but edits a
project copy from three months ago.
Tests succeed in that old copy, while the actual system
remains unchanged.
The execution environment includes the actual computer,
container, operating system, directory, software packages and
network.
A correct command does not establish that it ran in the
correct location.
5. Security: what is the engineer allowed to access?
Suppose you ask the engineer to repair the study planner, but
their permissions also allow reading the company payroll
database and deleting other projects.
Those permissions are excessive even if the engineer has no
malicious intent.
Security is like office access control. Permission to change
the study-planner project does not grant access to other data.
Saying “do not open that door” does not mean the door is
locked.
6. Observability: how do you know the engineer finished?
Suppose the engineer reports, “Fixed, and the tests passed.”
You ask, “Which file changed? Which test ran? On which version
The engineer cannot answer.
Observability provides work records and monitoring so you can
inspect executed commands, diffs, errors and test results.
An AI saying it finished is a claim; execution records and
test evidence make that claim checkable.
Check the working location, access boundaries and evidence:
where execution happens, which data can be accessed and how
results can be verified.
